blocks.text: Most mornings, before I decide whether to bring the board, the towel or just my coffee, I check a live surf cam. Bondi is a roughly one-kilometre crescent that faces south-east, so a single glance at the screen tells me the swell, the wind and how packed the sand already is. Here are the feeds I actually trust and how I read them.
There's no single "official" Bondi cam - a handful of feeds point at the beach, each with its own angle:
Swellnet - my first check. A live HD look across the beach paired with the current surf report, swell and wind. It's the one I'd send a visiting mate.
Surfline - another solid live cam bundled with a multi-day swell, wind and tide forecast. Handy when you're planning a few days ahead.
Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club - a stream from the club at the south end, above the corner where the surfers gather. It's the world's oldest surf lifesaving club, founded here in 1907.
North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club - a free community feed over the northern end, tucked under the Ben Buckler headland and usually the gentler side for a swim.

blocks.title: Streams move around
blocks.text: Cam operators occasionally change hosting, drop offline for maintenance, or move a feed behind a subscription. If a link's dead, open the club or Swellnet/Surfline homepage and follow their current cam link rather than trusting an old bookmark.
Reading the picture before you leave
A cam is a brilliant gut-check, but it flattens the ocean - waves always look smaller on a screen than they feel in the shorebreak. What I look for:
Watch a few sets roll through, not one frame, then cross-check against the swell and wind numbers. Bondi picks up south and east swell, and a light offshore westerly is what cleans it up.
The southern end near the point holds the better banks but draws the biggest crowd; the north end under Ben Buckler is the calmer choice for a straightforward swim.
Find the red-and-yellow flags on the cam - that patrolled strip is the only place you should swim. A darker, calmer channel cutting seaward through the whitewater is often a rip.
Glare is real. Around sunrise the low sun blows out the east-facing feeds, and after dark most are useless. Mid-morning gives the clearest read of both the surf and the crowd.

blocks.title: A cam is not a lifeguard
blocks.text: Never let a calm-looking screen talk you into swimming outside the flags or when the beach isn't patrolled. Conditions change fast and rips don't always show on camera. Confirm current patrol times and safety alerts on Surf Life Saving NSW's Beachsafe page, and ask a lifeguard on the sand if you're unsure.

items.q: Where can I watch a live Bondi Beach surf cam?
items.a: The most reliable free live feeds are the Swellnet and Surfline Bondi cams, plus community streams from the Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club (south end) and North Bondi Surf Life Saving Club. Each looks at a slightly different stretch of the beach.

items.q: Is the Bondi surf cam free to watch?
items.a: Watching the live streams is generally free. Some platforms put HD, replays or long-range forecasts behind a paid subscription, but you don't need to pay just to check current conditions.

items.q: Can I rely on the cam to decide it's safe to swim?
items.a: No. Use it as a first look, then always swim between the red-and-yellow flags during patrol hours and check current patrol times on Surf Life Saving NSW's Beachsafe page. A camera can't spot every rip.
